headline: US and Iran reignite their war over the Strait of Hormuz: Trump drops a 20% shipping fee but presses a naval blockade as strikes fly, pushing oil to a one-month high.
the_big_picture: The single thread running through today is the re-escalation of the US-Iran conflict at the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. Trump backed off a threatened 20% transit fee but is pushing ahead with a naval blockade while both sides trade strikes and tankers come under attack, sending crude to a one-month high. That oil spike is the hinge for everything downstream: US inflation cooled to 3.5% but officials flagged fresh upside risk, India's inflation just breached its central bank's target, the rupee slid past 96 and the Sensex fell. Running underneath, an AI storyline cuts both ways: IBM shed roughly $70bn in a day after stumbling on AI deals, even as China's AI-driven exports jumped 27% and Nvidia began shipping powerful H200 chips into China.

stories.title: Nevada clears Tesla, Uber and Waymo to run thousands of robotaxis in Las Vegas
key_points: Nevada's transportation regulator **unanimously approved** permits letting **Tesla, Uber and Waymo** run paid driverless rides across **Clark County**, home to Las Vegas.
Combined, the three companies can deploy up to **7,000 driverless vehicles** — Tesla alone cleared for **5,000**, Waymo and Uber **1,000 each**.
That's a massive jump from Tesla's earlier Nevada permit, which had capped its robotaxi fleet at just **10 vehicles** while regulators watched safety data.
Commercial rides are expected to start within **30 days**, still pending vehicle inspections, insurance filings and fare approval.
The approved numbers are a **ceiling, not a target** — even Tesla's own robotaxi engineering lead has called the 5,000 figure a cap, not a deployment plan.
stories.background: A robotaxi is a car that drives itself and picks up paying passengers with no human driver on board (or, in some current deployments, a human safety monitor). Waymo, owned by Google's parent Alphabet, has run driverless taxis commercially for several years in cities like Phoenix and San Francisco; Tesla has been racing to catch up with its own robotaxi service, while Uber has increasingly partnered with autonomous-vehicle makers rather than building its own self-driving tech. Nevada, and Clark County specifically, has become a proving ground for scaling these services because of relatively favorable state regulation and Las Vegas's dense tourist traffic. Tesla had only recently been granted a small pilot permit for just 10 vehicles in the state, so this approval represents a rapid escalation once regulators reviewed the safety case.
stories.what_happened: Nevada's transportation authority voted this week to approve commercial robotaxi permits for all three companies, authorizing Tesla to run up to 5,000 vehicles and Waymo and Uber up to 1,000 each — a combined ceiling of roughly 7,000 driverless cars in the Las Vegas region over the next 12 months. Uber's allotment will be operated through its partnerships with autonomous-driving firms Motional and Zoox rather than Uber's own self-driving technology. The approval covers paid commercial rides, not just testing, but companies still need to clear vehicle inspections, insurance filings and fare-structure approval before actually putting cars on the road — a process expected to take about 30 days. Analysts and even Tesla's own robotaxi chief engineer have cautioned that the approved numbers are upper limits the companies are unlikely to hit immediately, not confirmed near-term fleet sizes.
stories.why_it_matters: This makes Las Vegas one of the first US markets where three major robotaxi operators — Tesla, Waymo, and Uber's AV partners — will compete head-to-head at real commercial scale, rather than one company running a limited pilot. How that competition and safety record plays out will shape whether other states move as quickly to open their roads to driverless ride-hailing.
stories.ripple_effects: Local taxi and rideshare drivers face new competition from driverless fleets; insurers and regulators get a real-world stress test of how liability works when something goes wrong with no human driver to blame. For investors, the news reinforces the market narrative around Tesla's robotaxi ambitions and Alphabet's Waymo lead, and could influence how both stocks are valued on their self-driving bets.
stories.why_now: The vote happened this week after months of smaller pilot programs, and it's news now because it marks the shift from limited testing to a much larger commercial framework — with rides expected to start within 30 days.
stories.watch_next: Whether Tesla, Uber and Waymo actually begin paid rides within the 30-day window, and how large their real fleets are relative to the new caps in the first weeks.

key_terms.definition: A self-driving car that offers paid rides to the public, typically with no human driver in the vehicle.

stories.the_lesson: A regulatory approval sets the maximum a company is allowed to do, not what it will actually do — headline permit numbers are worth reading skeptically until real-world deployment catches up.
stories.market_link: Tesla (TSLA), Uber (UBER) and Alphabet (GOOGL, Waymo's parent) are all directly exposed — expanded Las Vegas permits feed the market narrative around each company's robotaxi strategy.

stories.title: Iran vows it 'will not submit' as Trump's Monday sanctions deadline looms and US gas prices climb

thread.previously: Treasury Secretary Bessent had announced a Monday press conference to unveil what he called among the toughest sanctions ever imposed on any nation, aiming for the "greatest coordinated economic isolation in history" and telling even China it would have to choose between trading with Iran or the US.
thread.changed: With the deadline now a day away, a close ally of Iran's supreme leader publicly rejected the pressure campaign, saying Iran "will not submit," while new reporting shows the standoff already pushing US gasoline prices up nearly $1 a gallon versus a year ago as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz stays low.

key_points: A senior ally of Iran's supreme leader said Trump's rhetoric reflects **desperation** and that Iran **"will not submit."**
The US is set to detail a new sanctions package **Monday**, part of what Treasury Secretary Bessent calls an **"economic D-Day."**
US gas prices are already up **nearly $1 a gallon** year-over-year, averaging **$4.11**, as Hormuz shipping traffic stays depressed.
Iran's Foreign Ministry called the sanctions threat a **"return to colonialism"** and an overreach of US authority over other sovereign states.
The State Department has already sanctioned **six entities and one individual** accused of moving Iranian funds via crypto, ahead of Monday's bigger move.
stories.background: The US and Iran have been locked in an escalating standoff for months, following a period of open conflict earlier in 2026 that included US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear and military sites. Talks over a new deal have repeatedly stalled, and Trump has increasingly leaned on economic pressure — casting it as a way to force Tehran back to the table without further military action. Iran, meanwhile, has leaned on the argument that decades of prior US sanctions never forced it to capitulate before.
stories.what_happened: A close ally of Iran's supreme leader **Ali Khamenei** said Friday that Trump's escalating rhetoric about the standoff stems from **desperation**, not strength, and vowed Iran **"will not submit"** to the coming pressure campaign. The comment came as the Trump administration confirmed it will detail a sweeping new round of Iran sanctions on **Monday**, following Trump's earlier vow of an **"economic D-Day"** and **"tremendous economic consequences"** for any country still doing business with Tehran. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson **Esmaeil Baghaei** called the threat **"a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism"** and an illegal assertion of US authority over other UN member states. Separately, CNN reported the **national average US gas price hit $4.11 a gallon** on Friday — up 97 cents from a year earlier — as shipping traffic through the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway that a fifth of the world's oil passes through, remains well below normal.
stories.why_it_matters: A sanctions push this sweeping doesn't just squeeze Iran — it forces every bank, shipping company, and government still trading with Tehran to choose between that business and access to the US financial system, turning a bilateral standoff into a global compliance problem. It's also already showing up at the gas pump for ordinary Americans, months before Monday's announcement even lands.
stories.ripple_effects: If Monday's sanctions target shipping and insurance networks, expect further disruption to Hormuz tanker traffic and upward pressure on global oil and gasoline prices. Countries like China and India, both large buyers of discounted Iranian crude, face a harder choice about continuing that trade versus keeping access to US banks and markets — a decision with real economic consequences either way.
stories.why_now: Monday marks the deadline Bessent set last week for unveiling the new sanctions package, and Iran's public defiance is a direct response to that approaching deadline.
stories.watch_next: Monday's Treasury press conference detailing the actual sanctions targets — and whether Iran responds with further threats against shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

key_terms.definition: A narrow shipping channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply passes through — disruption there tends to move global oil prices.

stories.the_lesson: Sanctions on one country routinely become a compliance decision for everyone who trades with it — which is exactly what makes them powerful, and why they tend to raise prices well beyond the target nation's borders.
stories.market_link: US gasoline already averages $4.11/gallon, up ~$1 year-over-year, on constrained Hormuz shipping; Monday's sanctions announcement is a near-term catalyst that could push crude and gasoline prices higher still, especially if it targets tanker insurers or shipping networks.

stories.title: A federal judge strikes down Trump's ban on visas for 75 countries as illegal
key_points: Judge **Jeannette Vargas** ruled the visa suspension **"contrary to law"** and beyond the State Department's authority.
The ban, launched in January, blocked **immigrant visas** for people from 75 countries deemed likely to become a **"public charge."**
The court said the policy illegally **discriminated by nationality**, violating a 1965 immigration law.
The ruling orders the State Department to go back to **case-by-case** visa review instead of blanket nationality bans.
The **Trump administration can still appeal**, and has not said whether it will.
stories.background: In January 2026, the US State Department announced it would stop issuing immigrant visas — the kind that lead to a **green card**, not tourist or student visas — to nationals of 75 countries, arguing they were at high risk of becoming a **"public charge"** (needing government welfare support). Immigrant-rights groups, visa applicants, and US citizens with foreign relatives sued, arguing the policy was really a blanket, nationality-based ban dressed up as an economic screening rule. The case, filed in the Southern District of New York, has been working through the courts for months while families stayed separated and pending visas sat frozen.
stories.what_happened: On Friday, **US District Judge Jeannette Vargas** ruled that Secretary of State **Marco Rubio's** 75-country visa suspension was **"contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority."** The court held that the policy violates a section of the **Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965** that explicitly bars the government from discriminating by nationality when issuing visas. Vargas vacated every visa denial that was based solely on the ban and ordered the State Department to restore **individual, case-by-case evaluation** of applications instead of a blanket nationality filter. A State Department spokesperson said the administration is "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening," and declined to comment further on ongoing litigation. The administration has not confirmed whether it will appeal the ruling.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a federal court telling the executive branch it overstepped its legal authority on immigration — a real check on how far a president can go without Congress. For the thousands of families and workers from the 75 affected countries, it reopens a path to visas that had been frozen for seven months.
stories.ripple_effects: Immigration lawyers expect a wave of previously-denied applicants to refile immediately, though processing backlogs mean relief won't be instant. If the administration appeals, the fight likely heads to the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals, and a stay pending appeal could freeze the reopened process again within weeks. The case also sets a precedent other courts may lean on if Washington tries similar nationality-based restrictions elsewhere, including on work visas.
stories.why_now: The ruling landed Friday after months of litigation, right as the case reached a decision point on the government's motion to dismiss the challenge.
stories.watch_next: Whether the State Department appeals or files for an emergency stay in the coming days, which would pause the reopened visa processing.

key_terms.definition: A visa that lets someone move to the US permanently and eventually become a green-card holder — different from a tourist or student visa, which are temporary.
A US immigration-law term for someone judged likely to depend primarily on government assistance; being labelled one can be grounds to deny a visa.

stories.the_lesson: Executive-branch policies — even ones framed as routine "screening" — still have to fit inside the specific powers Congress wrote into the law; courts can and do unwind them when they don't.
stories.market_link: Loosens a bottleneck that has hit skilled-worker and family visas for applicants from many of the 75 listed countries, including several with large diasporas in the US — a small positive for outbound remittances and family-linked flows if it survives an appeal.

stories.title: E. coli and Salmonella outbreak tied to alfalfa sprouts grows to 55 sick across 15 states
key_points: **55 people** across **15 US states** have been infected in a multistate outbreak linked to raw alfalfa sprouts.
The cases split as **46 with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli**, **7 with Salmonella**, and **2 infected with both**.
**4 people have been hospitalized**; no deaths have been reported so far.
The FDA traced the source to **Calco and Everything Sprouts-brand alfalfa sprouts**, made by Everything Sprouts LLC of Minneapolis, and has recalled them.
Illness onset dates range from **May 31 to August 8**, meaning the outbreak has been building for weeks before the public warning.
stories.background: Raw sprouts — alfalfa, clover, mung bean and similar varieties — are one of the most consistent repeat offenders in US foodborne illness outbreaks. That's because sprouts are grown in warm, humid conditions for several days, which is ideal not just for the seed to germinate but for any bacteria on it to multiply rapidly; unlike most vegetables, sprouts are typically eaten raw, so there's no cooking step to kill off contamination. The FDA and CDC jointly investigate these outbreaks, using genetic fingerprinting of the bacteria found in sick patients to link cases across different states to a single contaminated source.
stories.what_happened: The CDC and FDA have been investigating a multistate outbreak of **Shiga toxin-producing E. coli and Salmonella Agona** infections tied to alfalfa sprouts. On August 21, the FDA posted a formal outbreak advisory identifying **Everything Sprouts, LLC of Minneapolis, Minnesota** as the source, after tracing sickened patients back to its Calco and Everything Sprouts-brand alfalfa sprouts. As of the latest update, **55 people have fallen ill across 15 states**, with **4 hospitalizations** and no deaths reported. The affected products have been recalled, and health authorities are telling consumers not to eat, sell or serve them. Investigators note the actual case count is likely higher, since mild cases often go unreported and there's typically a lag between illness and being counted in official tallies.
stories.why_it_matters: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli can cause severe illness including kidney failure in vulnerable patients, particularly young children and the elderly, even though most cases resolve without hospitalization. Recurring sprout-linked outbreaks have pushed food-safety advocates to repeatedly call for tighter seed-disinfection and testing rules on growers — this is a live test of whether current FDA oversight catches contamination fast enough.
stories.ripple_effects: Grocery chains across the 15 affected states have to pull the recalled product from shelves, and consumers who bought it are being told to check their fridges and discard or return it. Expect a fresh round of scrutiny on sprout-growing practices industry-wide, and possibly copycat recalls if the contamination is traced to a shared seed supplier.
stories.why_now: The FDA's outbreak advisory and recall notice were only made public on August 21, even though the earliest illnesses date back to May — the delay reflects how long it takes to link scattered individual cases into a confirmed multistate outbreak.
stories.watch_next: Whether the case count keeps climbing as more state health departments report in, and whether investigators can pin down exactly where in the growing or distribution chain the contamination happened.

key_terms.definition: A strain of E. coli bacteria that produces a toxin capable of causing severe stomach illness and, in serious cases, kidney damage — distinct from the harmless E. coli that normally lives in the gut.

stories.the_lesson: The riskiest foods aren't always the ones you'd expect — a food's growing conditions and whether it's eaten raw or cooked often matter more for safety than how 'natural' or 'healthy' it seems.

stories.title: Magnitude-5.9 earthquake rattles Tokyo region, triggers liquefaction warnings for 20,000
key_points: A **magnitude-5.9 earthquake** struck southern Ibaraki Prefecture at **2am local time**, shaking Tokyo, Saitama and Chiba.
**Soil liquefaction warnings** were issued for more than **20,000 residents** on low-lying, reclaimed land.
The quake struck at a depth of roughly **61-70km** and registered **lower-5 intensity** on Japan's 7-point shindo scale in parts of Tokyo.
A **magnitude-4.4 aftershock** followed within hours; Japan's meteorological agency issued **no tsunami warning**.
About **36 million people** live within 100km of the epicenter — the world's most populous metropolitan area.
stories.background: Japan sits where the **Pacific, Philippine Sea and Eurasian tectonic plates** grind against each other, making it one of the most earthquake-prone countries on Earth — it records thousands of quakes a year, most too small to feel. Since the devastating **2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami**, Japan has poured money into some of the world's strictest seismic building codes and a nationwide early-warning system that gives residents seconds to brace before shaking arrives. Much of Tokyo Bay's shoreline, including parts of Chiba and Saitama, sits on reclaimed or soft alluvial land, which is especially prone to **liquefaction** — when shaking causes waterlogged soil to temporarily behave like a liquid, making buildings tilt or sink.
stories.what_happened: The earthquake struck at about 2am local time on Sunday, centered in southern Ibaraki Prefecture, just north of the greater Tokyo area. Japan's meteorological agency measured it at **magnitude 5.8-5.9** at a depth of roughly 61-70km. Shaking was felt as far as Tokyo's Adachi Ward, Saitama and Chiba, registering **lower-5 on Japan's 7-point shindo intensity scale** — strong enough to wake residents and rattle furniture, but well short of the intensities that cause serious structural damage. Authorities issued **liquefaction warnings for over 20,000 residents** in vulnerable low-lying areas. A **magnitude-4.4 aftershock** hit in the following hours, and several smaller aftershocks were recorded. No tsunami warning was issued, and no deaths or serious injuries have been reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Greater Tokyo is Japan's economic and financial nerve center and the most populous metro area on the planet — even a moderate quake tests transit systems, supply chains and building resilience for tens of millions of people. It's also a reminder of the much larger risk seismologists have long warned about: a direct hit on Tokyo from a major fault could be catastrophic, and Japan's government treats every quake like this as a data point for that scenario.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect brief train service checks and delays across Tokyo's rail network (standard safety protocol after any quake above a certain intensity), and renewed local debate about reinforcing reclaimed-land neighborhoods against liquefaction. Japanese insurers and reinsurers, who price earthquake risk into everything from home policies to catastrophe bonds, will log this as a minor, contained event rather than a market-moving one.
stories.why_now: No single trigger — Japan's seismic activity is a constant background risk, and quakes of this size near Tokyo happen every few years without escalating further.
stories.watch_next: Japan's meteorological agency will watch the aftershock sequence over the next 24-48 hours for any sign of a larger follow-up quake, and local authorities will publish damage and liquefaction assessments.

key_terms.definition: When intense shaking causes water-saturated, loose soil to briefly behave like a liquid, making the ground unstable and causing buildings or pipes to sink or tilt even without violent shaking damage.
Japan's 7-point earthquake intensity scale (0 to 7) measuring how strongly shaking is felt at a specific location, as opposed to magnitude, which measures the quake's total energy at its source.

stories.the_lesson: In a country with strict building codes and early-warning systems, a moderate earthquake near a megacity causes disruption, not catastrophe — preparedness narrows the gap between a quake's raw magnitude and the damage it actually does.

stories.title: Bitcoin surges 22% in a week to near $80,000 as Trump pushes crypto legislation
key_points: **Bitcoin** closed the week up **22%** — its best week in two years — ending Friday around **$77,700** after briefly touching near **$80,000**.
The rally followed President **Trump** meeting crypto executives at the White House and pushing Congress to pass the **CLARITY Act**, a bill to set clearer US crypto market rules.
Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** added fuel by announcing plans to **double long-term bond buyback limits**, easing bond-market stress that had been dragging on risk assets.
The rally triggered a **short squeeze**: roughly **$2.7 billion** in crypto short positions were forcibly liquidated as prices spiked.
**Ethereum** climbed above **$2,200** and **XRP jumped 25%**, while spot Bitcoin ETFs pulled in **$517 million** in a single day of net inflows.
stories.background: Crypto markets had been stuck in a **months-long slump** for much of mid-2026, weighed down by a broader sell-off in US government bonds (Treasurys) that pushed yields higher and made investors more cautious about risky assets like crypto. The **CLARITY Act** is a proposed US law meant to spell out which US regulator (the SEC or the CFTC) oversees which crypto assets — the current murky rules have been a long-standing complaint from the industry, which says it deters institutional investment. President Trump has positioned himself as broadly pro-crypto since taking office.
stories.what_happened: Bitcoin rallied hard through the week, closing Friday with a **22% weekly gain** — its best week in two years — after briefly challenging the **$80,000** level overnight before settling near **$77,700**. The catalyst was twofold: Trump met with crypto industry executives at the White House and publicly urged Congress to pass the CLARITY Act, and separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the government would **double its long-term bond buyback limits**, which calmed the bond market stress that had been pressuring risk assets all month. The sudden move upward forced traders who had bet on falling prices to close out their positions, triggering a **short squeeze** that liquidated roughly **$2.7 billion** in short bets, according to data from CoinGlass. The rally spread across the sector: Ethereum broke above $2,200, XRP jumped 25%, and spot Bitcoin ETFs — funds that let ordinary investors hold Bitcoin through a regular brokerage account — took in **$517 million** of new money in a single day.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a sharp reversal after months of crypto underperformance, and it shows how sensitive crypto prices are to both US regulatory clarity and to broader bond-market conditions. A short squeeze of this size ($2.7B) also mechanically amplifies the move, meaning part of the rally is forced buying rather than pure conviction.
stories.ripple_effects: Crypto-adjacent stocks — trading platforms like Robinhood and Coinbase — jumped alongside the rally. If the CLARITY Act advances in Congress, it could unlock further institutional investment into crypto; if bond-market stress returns, risk assets including crypto would likely give back these gains quickly given how leveraged the move was.
stories.why_now: The rally is a direct reaction to two same-week catalysts — Trump's White House push on crypto legislation and Bessent's bond buyback announcement — landing on a market that was already coiled after a prolonged slump, which amplified the move into a short squeeze.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether the CLARITY Act actually advances through Congress in the coming weeks, and whether bond yields stay calm — both were direct triggers for this rally and could just as easily reverse it.

key_terms.definition: When traders who bet an asset's price will fall are forced to buy it back as the price rises instead, and that forced buying pushes the price up even further.
When a government repurchases some of its own previously issued debt, which can ease pressure in the bond market and indirectly make other assets look more attractive.

stories.the_lesson: Sharp, fast rallies are often not pure investor conviction — they can be mechanically amplified by forced buying (short squeezes) once a market that was leaning heavily one way gets a surprise catalyst in the other direction.
stories.market_link: Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, spot Bitcoin ETFs, and crypto-exposed equities (Robinhood, Coinbase) all moved sharply higher on this news.

stories.title: Tesla recalls nearly 3 million EVs in China as regulators crack down on hidden door handles
key_points: Tesla is recalling almost **3 million vehicles** in China — mostly Model 3 and Model Y — over **door handle safety risks**.
It's part of a broader crackdown covering more than **4 million vehicles**, one of the biggest recalls ever in the world's largest auto market.
Chinese regulators tightened rules after crashes where occupants **couldn't be extracted in time**, including EV fires after collisions.
In a severe crash, the low-voltage system can fail, jamming the electronic **flush door handles** shut from outside and in.
Tesla will add warning labels and push an **over-the-air software update** so windows auto-lower after a crash is detected.
stories.background: Many modern EVs, including Tesla's, use **flush, electronically-retracting door handles** for aerodynamics and styling — they sit flat against the body and pop out only when needed, powered by the car's electrical system. That design has drawn safety scrutiny globally because if the car's low-voltage electrical system fails (common in severe crashes or fires), the handles can become impossible to open from outside, delaying rescue. China, the world's biggest EV market, has been tightening vehicle-safety regulation this year following several incidents where crash victims could not be extracted quickly enough.
stories.what_happened: Tesla announced a recall covering just under **3 million vehicles** in China — primarily **2.98 million Model 3 and Model Y** cars, plus some Model S and Model X — as part of a nationwide crackdown affecting more than **4 million vehicles** from multiple automakers. Chinese regulators tightened rules on electronically controlled doors after incidents where people could not be extracted from crashed vehicles in time, in some cases contributing to deaths when EVs caught fire post-collision. Tesla's recall notice says a severe collision can cause the car's low-voltage electrical system to fail, which in turn can prevent doors from being opened quickly from either inside or outside, hindering both self-rescue and rescue by outside responders. Tesla's fix combines physical **warning labels** on the affected cars with an **over-the-air software update** that will make windows automatically lower once the car detects it has been in an accident.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest vehicle recalls ever in China, the world's biggest auto market, and it targets a design feature — flush electronic door handles — used widely across the EV industry, not just by Tesla, so it could push regulators and automakers globally to rethink the feature.
stories.ripple_effects: Other EV makers using similar flush-handle designs may face similar regulatory pressure in China and potentially other markets; the fix being a mostly-free software update limits the direct cost to Tesla, but the safety narrative could affect consumer trust in electronic door systems more broadly.
stories.why_now: The recall follows a documented pattern of crashes in China where occupants couldn't be extracted quickly because of failed electronic door handles, prompting regulators to force a sweeping, market-wide fix.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether regulators in other major markets (the US, Europe) follow China's lead and require similar fixes for flush door handles across the EV industry.

key_terms.definition: An electronically retracting door handle that sits flat against the car body until needed, popping out on approach — used for aerodynamics and styling but reliant on the car's electrical system to work.

The car's standard 12V-style electrical system that powers basic functions like door locks and lights, separate from the high-voltage battery that drives the motor — if it fails, many electronic features (including door handles) can stop working.

stories.the_lesson: A design feature built for looks or efficiency (like flush handles) can become a serious safety liability if it depends on a system that can fail exactly when it's needed most — in a crash.
stories.market_link: Tesla (TSLA) and other EV makers selling flush-handle designs in China face potential recall costs and regulatory scrutiny.

stories.title: Russia hits a border crossing with Moldova for the first time in an overnight barrage that kills at least 7 in Ukraine
key_points: Russia fired a mass overnight barrage at **Kyiv and the surrounding region**.
Drones struck a **border crossing with Moldova** in Odesa Oblast, briefly shutting it down.
Ukraine says it downed or suppressed **3 ballistic missiles, 6 cruise missiles and 182 drones**.
At least **7 killed and 31 injured** nationwide, per the Kyiv Independent; tolls are still being confirmed.
Gas infrastructure in **Chernihiv region** was also targeted in the same wave.
stories.background: Russia's war on Ukraine, now in its fifth year, has increasingly relied on massed missile-and-drone barrages against cities and infrastructure rather than only front-line fighting. Recent weeks have already seen Russian strikes on Ukrainian e-commerce warehouses and a 'double-tap' hit on a shopping mall in President Zelensky's hometown. Moldova, a non-NATO country bordering Ukraine that is pursuing EU membership, has so far stayed outside direct fire, though stray drone debris has occasionally landed on its territory.
stories.what_happened: Overnight into August 22, Russia launched a large wave of drones and missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, while also striking gas infrastructure in Chernihiv region and — notably — hitting a border crossing point with Moldova in Odesa Oblast with a drone, temporarily shutting it before it was restored. Ukraine's air force said it intercepted or suppressed three ballistic missiles, six cruise missiles and 182 drones. President Zelensky and Ukrainian officials said the barrage killed at least 7 people and injured 31 across the country, with local tolls still being updated. Ukraine has continued its own counter-strikes on Russian oil and logistics targets in response.
stories.why_it_matters: Striking infrastructure at a border crossing with Moldova — a country not directly party to the war — signals Russia is willing to hit closer to the frontier of an EU-candidate state, raising fears the conflict's edges could widen even without troops crossing a new border.
stories.ripple_effects: The strikes add urgency to Ukraine's requests for more Western air-defense systems, could push EU discussion of security guarantees for Moldova, and keep energy and border infrastructure vulnerable heading toward another winter. Expect continued tit-for-tat strikes as Ukraine hits back at Russian oil and logistics sites.
stories.why_now: It's part of an intensifying pattern of large-scale Russian barrages through August 2026, coming just after Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed Ukrainian peace proposals as too 'exotic' — reducing near-term prospects for a ceasefire.
stories.watch_next: Whether Moldova or the EU formally protests the border-crossing strike, and whether Western allies respond with new air-defense pledges to Kyiv.

key_terms.definition: A nation formally in the process of negotiating to join the European Union — Moldova is one, which is part of why a strike near its border draws EU attention.

stories.the_lesson: Modern wars increasingly test targets right up to a neutral border — a warning sign that a conflict's risk of spillover can rise even without troops physically crossing a new frontier.
stories.market_link: Keeps a geopolitical risk premium in European natural-gas and grain markets, and adds pressure on currencies of countries near the conflict zone.

stories.title: Iran executes a protester convicted of 'spying for Israel' amid a wartime wave of hangings
key_points: **Majid Adineh** was executed early Sunday, per Iran's judiciary-linked Mizan news agency.
He was arrested in **January 2026** during nationwide anti-government protests in Karaj.
Convicted of **'operational actions' for Israel and the US** — a capital 'waging war against God' charge.
Iran's **Supreme Court upheld** the sentence on appeal; his property was also ordered confiscated.
Part of a **wider wave of wartime executions** since the 2026 Iran war began in February.
stories.background: Since the US and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on **February 28, 2026** — starting what's now called the **2026 Iran war** — Iran's government has been fighting an active, at-times-direct conflict with Israel and Washington. Domestically, the regime has responded to the unrest and dissent that followed with a wave of executions, framing detained protesters as foreign spies or saboteurs rather than as demonstrators. Majid Adineh was one of those swept up: arrested by Revolutionary Guard intelligence forces in the Mohammadshahr area of Karaj on **January 9, 2026**, during that month's protests.
stories.what_happened: Iran's judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported that Majid Adineh was executed early Sunday, August 23. The Karaj Revolutionary Court had convicted him of carrying out 'operational actions' on behalf of **Israel, the US, and hostile groups**, alongside charges of arson, conspiracy against internal security, and illegal weapons possession — charges Iran's legal system files under **moharebeh** ('waging war against God'), a capital offense. Iran's Supreme Court upheld the death sentence on appeal and ordered his property confiscated. His execution follows at least two other men executed on similar espionage charges earlier in August, as the pace of wartime hangings has picked up.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows Iran's government using the wartime state of emergency to intensify domestic repression, conflating ordinary protest activity with foreign espionage to justify capital punishment. That raises the human cost of the 2026 Iran war well beyond the battlefield.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect renewed condemnation from international human-rights groups tracking a rising execution toll tied to the January 2026 unrest. It may also harden Western resolve behind the fresh Iran sanctions Washington has signaled this week, even as it risks fueling more domestic anger over what critics call show-trial justice.
stories.why_now: The execution lands as the broader Iran war grinds on and just days after the US Treasury signaled unprecedented new sanctions on Iran — the crackdown looks like the regime projecting control at home even as it faces mounting pressure abroad.
stories.watch_next: Whether international rights monitors publish an updated execution count tied to the January 2026 crackdown, and whether the pace of hangings continues alongside the sanctions standoff.

key_terms.definition: An Islamic legal charge meaning 'waging war against God' — used in Iran to justify the death penalty for offenses the state deems a threat to its security.

stories.the_lesson: During wartime, governments sometimes use national-security charges to fast-track punishment for domestic dissent — recognizing that pattern helps you separate a genuine security threat from a crackdown on protest.
stories.market_link: Adds to the geopolitical risk premium already priced into oil markets amid the broader Iran standoff and the looming new US sanctions.

stories.title: TikTok and ByteDance agree to pay $400 million to settle a US children's-privacy lawsuit
key_points: TikTok and parent company **ByteDance** will pay **$400 million** to settle a 2024 lawsuit over illegally collecting children's data.
The Justice Department calls it **one of the largest recoveries ever** secured in a children's-privacy case.
TikTok pays **$300 million immediately**, and another **$100 million** once a related 2019 court order against predecessor app Musical.ly is lifted.
The lawsuit alleged TikTok let children under 13 sign up and **collected their personal data** without parental consent, violating US law known as **COPPA**.
The settlement resolves the case **without TikTok admitting wrongdoing**, typical of large corporate settlements.
stories.background: The US Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, known as **COPPA**, requires apps to get a parent's permission before collecting personal data from anyone under 13. TikTok's earlier version, Musical.ly, was already penalized for violating this law back in 2019 and placed under a court order requiring it to fix its practices. The Justice Department sued TikTok and ByteDance again in **2024**, alleging the company kept letting underage children onto the platform and kept harvesting their data anyway. The settlement lands while TikTok is separately fighting a much higher-stakes political battle in Washington over its Chinese ownership.
stories.what_happened: On **August 22, 2026**, the US Department of Justice announced TikTok and ByteDance agreed to pay **$400 million** to end a lawsuit first filed in 2024 over children's privacy. The suit alleged the app failed to stop children under 13 from creating accounts and then unlawfully collected their personal data, violating **COPPA**. Under the settlement, TikTok pays **$300 million immediately**, with the remaining **$100 million** due once a court formally lifts an earlier 2019 consent decree tied to Musical.ly. The DOJ called it **one of the largest recoveries ever secured in a COPPA case**. The deal closes the litigation without a trial and without TikTok admitting fault.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a rare case of the US government extracting a nine-figure penalty from a major tech platform over how it treats children's data, at a time when regulators worldwide are still figuring out how to police kids' safety online. It also shows that even as TikTok fights its bigger political battle over ownership, ordinary privacy law still has real teeth to constrain it.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect other platforms popular with teens and children — short-video apps, gaming platforms, AI chatbot services — to face more scrutiny under COPPA now that this settlement sets a size benchmark. It could also strengthen the hand of US lawmakers pushing to update children's online-safety law, since $400 million is being cited as proof current rules bite when enforced.
stories.why_now: The case has moved through the courts since 2024, and the settlement lands as TikTok separately navigates its high-profile fight in Washington over Chinese ownership — a moment when both sides have an incentive to resolve smaller disputes quietly.
stories.watch_next: Watch for whether the court formally vacates the 2019 Musical.ly consent decree, which triggers the second **$100 million** payment.

key_terms.definition: the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, a US law requiring apps and websites to get parental consent before collecting data from children under 13.
a legally binding agreement, approved by a court, requiring a company to change its behavior — breaking one can trigger fresh penalties.

stories.the_lesson: Regulators often can't stop a company's biggest strategic risk directly, but narrower rules like child-privacy law still let them extract real money and real behavior change even while the bigger fight continues elsewhere.
stories.market_link: TikTok/ByteDance isn't publicly listed, but the size of this settlement is a data point on regulatory risk for social-media and AI companies more broadly — relevant to how investors price legal overhang on Big Tech.

stories.title: A sword attack at a reopened Swedish school kills a 17-year-old girl, its own student the suspect
key_points: An **18-year-old former student** returned to Brinell School in Fagersta, Sweden with a sword and attacked people just as the new term began.
A **17-year-old girl was killed**; two boys, aged 12 and 17, were **seriously wounded**, and a third victim was slightly hurt.
Police **fired shots** while detaining the suspect, who was not hit, and are investigating on suspicion of **murder and attempted murder**.
Officials say there is **no evidence anyone else was involved**, treating it as an isolated act rather than a coordinated attack.
The attack reopens Sweden's debate over **school security and youth violence**, following years of rising gang-linked crime among minors.
stories.background: Sweden has spent the past decade grappling with a rise in youth violence, much of it tied to criminal gangs recruiting teenagers because minors face lighter legal penalties than adults. But an attack carried out inside a school, by one of its own former students, is far rarer and tends to trigger nationwide alarm. Brinell School in Fagersta, a small industrial town northwest of Stockholm, had just reopened after summer break — for many students, Friday was literally their first day back. The suspect, aged 18, reportedly attended the school, meaning he had inside knowledge of its layout and daily routine.
stories.what_happened: On Friday, August 21, an **18-year-old man armed with a sword** entered Brinell School in Fagersta, northwest of Stockholm, and attacked people while classes were in session. A **17-year-old girl was killed**, and two boys — aged 12 and 17 — were **seriously injured**; a third, younger victim suffered minor injuries and was treated and released. Police responded quickly, **fired shots** during the arrest, and took the suspect into custody uninjured. Investigators say the attacker was himself a student at the school and that they have **no reason to believe anyone else was involved**. The case is being investigated as murder and attempted murder, and it occurred on the school's very first day back from summer recess.
stories.why_it_matters: A student turning a weapon on classmates and staff, on the day school reopens, shakes public trust in the safety of everyday spaces. It feeds into a wider European conversation about **spotting and intervening with at-risk teenagers before violence happens**, not just responding after the fact.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect Swedish schools and municipalities to review **entry security and staff training** in the coming weeks, echoing debates that follow similar incidents elsewhere in Europe. The case will likely reignite political arguments in Sweden over **youth crime policy**, already high on the agenda because of gang-related violence, and could shape how schools handle students previously flagged as troubled.
stories.why_now: The attack happened on the school's reopening day after summer break, when campuses are fuller and less on alert than during a normal term, and follows months of Swedish political focus on rising youth violence more broadly.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the results of the police investigation into the suspect's motive and whether he or the school had prior contact flagged with authorities.

key_terms.definition: the pattern of criminal networks enlisting teenagers because, under many countries' laws, minors face lighter penalties than adults for the same crimes.

stories.the_lesson: When a violent act happens inside a place built on trust and routine, like a school, the social shock it causes often outweighs the statistical rarity of the event — and that shock, not just the raw numbers, is usually what drives policy change.

stories.title: JWST finds early-universe galaxies were hiding huge populations of faint stars — some may be 4x heavier than thought
key_points: The **James Webb Space Telescope** found far more small, faint stars in early galaxies than models predicted.
At least one galaxy could be **3-4x more massive** than previously calculated.
The findings challenge the **"initial mass function"** — the standard formula astronomers use to estimate a galaxy's mass from its light.
The study examined **nine massive, dormant galaxies** from the early universe using deep JWST spectra.
It deepens a known puzzle: how did the universe build such large, mature galaxies **so soon after the Big Bang?**
stories.background: Astronomers can't count stars in distant galaxies one by one — instead, they measure a galaxy's total light and use a standard formula, the **initial mass function (IMF)**, to estimate how much of that light comes from big bright stars versus small dim ones, and from that infer the galaxy's total mass. This formula was built largely from studying nearby, modern galaxies like our own Milky Way, on the assumption it applies everywhere and every era. Since JWST launched, it has repeatedly found galaxies in the early universe that look unexpectedly large and mature for how soon after the Big Bang they formed, straining existing models of galaxy formation.
stories.what_happened: A team from Leiden University and Penn State used JWST's NIRSpec instrument to take deep spectra of **nine massive, "quiescent" galaxies** — ones that have stopped forming new stars — from the early universe. They found these galaxies contain far more small, faint, low-mass stars than the standard initial mass function predicts, a "bottom-heavy" star population. Because these faint stars are hard to detect but numerous, accounting for them properly means some of these galaxies could be **3 to 4 times more massive** than earlier estimates suggested. The research was published in *Nature Astronomy* and widely reported on August 22, 2026.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a genuine "our models are wrong" moment: astronomers have been using one formula to estimate the mass of virtually every galaxy they study, and this finding suggests that formula breaks down for the early universe. It matters because a galaxy's estimated mass feeds directly into theories about how fast galaxies can form and grow after the Big Bang.
stories.ripple_effects: If early galaxies are systematically undercounted in mass, it worsens an existing tension in cosmology — models already struggle to explain how galaxies got so big, so fast, in the universe's early history. Expect follow-up studies re-examining other "impossibly massive" early galaxies JWST has spotted, and possible revisions to computer simulations of galaxy formation.
stories.why_now: The finding is surfacing now because it was published in Nature Astronomy and picked up widely by science outlets on August 22, following JWST's ongoing campaign of deep spectroscopic surveys of the early universe.
stories.watch_next: Watch for follow-up JWST spectroscopy of other "too massive, too early" galaxies to see if the bottom-heavy star pattern holds more broadly.

key_terms.definition: The standard formula astronomers use to estimate how many stars of each size exist in a galaxy, based on its total light — used to convert light into a mass estimate.
A galaxy that has largely stopped forming new stars, as opposed to an actively star-forming galaxy.

stories.the_lesson: Scientific models built from what we can easily observe nearby don't always hold up in extreme or distant environments — when new instruments let us look closer, long-standing assumptions can turn out to be systematically wrong, not just slightly off.

stories.title: Former Israeli PM Bennett warns Netanyahu's campaign could trigger violence against his rivals
key_points: Naftali Bennett, a former Israeli PM, called Netanyahu an **"anarchist"** and **"authoritarian"** on Channel 12.
Bennett warned Netanyahu's campaign machine could put rival **Gadi Eisenkot** in physical danger.
Israel heads to the polls on **October 27**, with Netanyahu's coalition under real pressure.
Eisenkot, a former **IDF chief of staff**, has emerged as the leading centrist challenger.
Bennett's own alliance with Yair Lapid has **slipped in the polls** ahead of the vote.
stories.background: Naftali Bennett was Israel's prime minister from 2021-2022, leading a fragile coalition that briefly ousted Netanyahu before it collapsed. He has since positioned himself as a centrist alternative, most recently teaming up with opposition figure **Yair Lapid**. Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military, has become a prominent post-war critic of Netanyahu's Gaza strategy and is now seen as a serious contender in the run-up to the **October 27 election**. Netanyahu's coalition has leaned on friendly media outlets like Channel 14 and allied social-media accounts to attack opponents throughout his tenure.
stories.what_happened: In a Channel 12 interview broadcast on **August 22**, timed to a new book about his time in office, Bennett accused Netanyahu of behaving like an **"anarchist"** who has **"forgotten how to be a democrat."** He said Netanyahu's campaign apparatus — Likud figures, Channel 14, and allied social-media accounts — is stoking a toxic climate that could lead to **physical violence against Eisenkot**, his most serious challenger. Bennett did not accuse Netanyahu of ordering violence directly, but said the rhetoric was creating dangerous conditions. The remarks land as Israel's political class is bracing for a bruising campaign season with the country's post-war direction — Gaza policy, the statehood question, and ongoing judicial fights — all on the ballot.
stories.why_it_matters: A former prime minister publicly warning that a sitting PM's campaign tactics could get a rival hurt is a serious escalation in Israeli politics, which has a painful history with political violence (Yitzhak Rabin's assassination in 1995 followed a similarly charged campaign climate). It signals just how polarized the run-up to the October election has become.
stories.ripple_effects: If the warning proves prescient, it could reshape how Israeli security services handle protection for opposition candidates and intensify scrutiny of incendiary rhetoric from partisan media. It also underscores how contested Netanyahu's political survival is after nearly three years of war — the election result will shape Israel's approach to Gaza, Iran, and its relationship with Washington.
stories.why_now: The warning surfaces now because Israel's formal election campaign is heating up ahead of the October 27 vote, and Bennett is promoting a new book that revisits his fraught relationship with Netanyahu.
stories.watch_next: Watch how Israeli security services respond and whether other political figures — across the spectrum — echo or reject Bennett's warning in the coming days.

key_terms.definition: The most senior officer in the Israel Defense Forces, roughly equivalent to a country's top military commander.

stories.the_lesson: When a country's own former leaders start warning publicly about political violence, it's usually a sign that democratic norms — not just policy disagreements — have become the actual battleground of an election.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO paperwork will warn investors that the AI backlash is a real risk to its business
key_points: Anthropic's coming **IPO prospectus** will list public backlash against AI as an official **risk factor**, per sources.
The company is privately valued near **$1 trillion**, with investors eyeing a public valuation near **$2 trillion**.
A **Gallup survey** found **7 in 10 Americans** oppose new AI data centers being built in their area.
The risk: backlash could **slow data-center construction**, directly threatening the compute Anthropic needs to keep growing.
Anthropic confidentially filed for its offering in **June**; the public prospectus is expected within weeks.
stories.background: Anthropic makes the Claude family of AI models and has grown into one of the most valuable private tech companies in the world, competing directly with OpenAI. Like other AI giants, its growth depends on building or renting enormous amounts of computing power — usually housed in energy-hungry **data centers**. As AI investment has surged, so has public unease: concerns about job losses, electricity and water use, noise, and rising local power bills have turned many communities against new data-center projects. Companies preparing to go public are legally required to disclose material risks to their business in IPO filings.
stories.what_happened: According to people familiar with the matter who spoke to CNBC, Anthropic's upcoming initial public offering (IPO) prospectus will explicitly name **negative public sentiment toward AI and data centers** as a risk factor for the company. The disclosure reflects growing concern that opposition to AI infrastructure could slow the pace at which new data centers get built — and Anthropic's revenue growth depends heavily on having enough computing capacity to train and run its models. The company, valued at close to **$1 trillion** in private markets, is reportedly eyeing a public listing that investors think could value it near **$2 trillion**. Anthropic filed confidentially for the offering in **June 2026**, and the full public filing is expected to appear within weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the most anticipated tech IPOs in years, and it's notable that the company itself is flagging public opposition to AI as a genuine financial risk — not just an activist talking point. It's a sign that the 'AI backlash' has become concrete enough to show up in legal risk disclosures, which only cover risks a company considers real and material.
stories.ripple_effects: If local opposition succeeds in slowing or blocking data-center permits, it could raise costs and delay capacity across the whole AI industry, not just Anthropic — affecting rivals like OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft too. It could also shape how investors price AI companies going forward, treating 'social license to build' as a genuine business risk alongside things like competition or regulation.
stories.why_now: The disclosure surfaces now because Anthropic is actively preparing its IPO paperwork, and securities law requires companies to disclose risks that could materially affect their business before they sell shares to the public.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Anthropic's public S-1 filing in the coming weeks, which will spell out the exact risk language and financial details for the first time.

key_terms.definition: The legal document a company must file before selling shares to the public, which includes a 'risk factors' section listing things that could hurt the business.
A large facility packed with computer servers, used to train and run AI models — these need huge amounts of electricity and water to operate and cool.

stories.the_lesson: When a company writes something into its official risk disclosures, it's a stronger signal than a press statement — regulators require these disclosures to be honest about real threats, so it's worth paying attention to what a business is willing to admit could hurt it.
stories.market_link: Relevant to AI-exposed stocks broadly (chipmakers, cloud providers, data-center REITs) and to any future Anthropic public shares; local backlash against data centers is an emerging cost/delay risk across the AI supply chain.

stories.title: Canada vows 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliation as US-Canada trade talks collapse and 50% tariffs land
key_points: Canadian PM **Mark Carney** said Canada will match the new US tariffs **dollar for dollar**, starting **September 8**.
The retaliation follows Friday's collapse of trade talks, after which Trump's **50% tariffs on ~$20 billion** of Canadian goods took effect.
Canada's countermeasures will target **steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics**.
Carney called the US move **'a miscalculation'**; exact product lists are still being finalized.
This is the sharpest escalation yet in a trade relationship that, until this year, was largely tariff-free under the old USMCA deal.
stories.background: The US and Canada have historically been each other's largest trading partners, with a decades-old free-trade relationship that kept most goods moving tariff-free. That changed as President Trump pushed a broader tariff agenda this year, and talks meant to carve out a new arrangement for Canada were still underway as of last week. A **midnight Friday deadline** for a deal passed without agreement, triggering the **50% US tariff** on a swath of Canadian exports including dairy, alcohol, cement, and hockey equipment.
stories.what_happened: Trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa collapsed on **Friday night**, just before a deadline that would trigger new US tariffs. Hours after midnight, the United States imposed **50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion** of Canadian goods. In response, Canadian Prime Minister **Mark Carney** announced that Canada would impose its own retaliatory tariffs on US goods starting **September 8**, matching the American tariffs **'dollar for dollar.'** Carney said the goal was to **'protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses,'** and that Canada's countermeasures would focus on sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. He added that further details on which specific products would be hit are still being worked out and will come in the following days.
stories.why_it_matters: Canada is one of America's largest trading partners, so a full tariff war between the two raises costs for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border — from car parts to groceries. It also signals that even close, long-standing US allies are not being spared from Trump's tariff strategy.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect price increases on cross-border goods like dairy, steel, and electronics in both countries, and pressure on manufacturers who rely on integrated US-Canada supply chains (especially autos). Canadian exporters in the newly tariffed sectors will look for other markets, while US industries that rely on Canadian steel or potash could face higher input costs. The dispute could also spill into other US trade fights, as other partners watch how firmly Canada — a traditional ally — pushes back.
stories.why_now: The escalation was triggered by a hard deadline: talks had to produce a deal by Friday midnight or the tariffs would automatically kick in, and no agreement was reached in time.
stories.watch_next: Watch for Canada's detailed tariff list in the coming days and whether Washington and Ottawa return to the table before the September 8 retaliation date.

key_terms.definition: A trade policy where a country imposes tariffs equal in value to the tariffs another country placed on it, rather than a fixed percentage.
The US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement that replaced NAFTA in 2020, which historically kept most trade between the three countries tariff-free.

stories.the_lesson: Tariff fights escalate fast once a deadline passes without a deal — each side's retaliation becomes the new baseline for the next round, which is why trade negotiators try hard to avoid letting talks run right up to a hard cutoff.
stories.market_link: Canadian steel, dairy, and electronics exporters, and US industries dependent on Canadian inputs (autos, potash-based fertilizer) are most exposed; watch the Canadian dollar and cross-border industrial stocks.
